variants.name: JMS/Jakarta time-to-live on the producer
variants.implementation_notes: The canonical JVM realization is declarative: send with MessageProducer.setTimeToLive(ms) or the three-argument send, and the provider stamps JMSExpiration = dispatch time + TTL on the message; when it is reached the provider should discard the message, and the specification defines no notification of expiration. Consumers can read getJMSExpiration() (zero meaning never expires) to re-check, and most brokers configure a dead-letter queue where expired messages can be inspected instead of vanishing. The producer TTL remains the right choice whenever the message crosses a broker, because the enforcement belongs to the messaging system; inside a single JVM use the DelayQueue realization instead.
pitfalls: JMSExpiration is computed from the sending host's wall clock and the spec defines no accuracy guarantee, so brokers expire lazily (often only on delivery or scan) and mounted consumers must not rely on the provider alone.

The producer-level default applies to every subsequent send and setTimeToLive(0) means unlimited; per-message expiry has to be passed on the send call itself, and a TTL set after sending cannot retroact.
Provider behaviour differs: some dead-letter expired messages, some discard them, and nothing in the API reports which happened - verify the broker's configuration rather than assuming.

variants.name: DelayQueue over the Delayed interface (in-process)
variants.implementation_notes: Inside one JVM the standard library supplies the whole mechanism: DelayQueue holds Delayed elements, orders them by the remaining delay that getDelay(TimeUnit) reports, and its blocking take() returns the head only once that delay has elapsed - so a single expiry thread is enough, no per-message timers. getDelay must be computed from a monotonic source (System.nanoTime) for the ordering to be stable under wall-clock adjustments, and the element itself carries the payload plus its deadline. Choose it when there is no broker and expiry must be exact on the consumer's own clock; keep JMS TTL when the message crosses processes.
pitfalls: getDelay must use a monotonic clock; mixing System.currentTimeMillis into both the deadline and getDelay lets a clock step reorder the queue or keep elements forever.
DelayQueue is unbounded and removes nothing by itself - whoever takes an expired element must decide to discard or dead-letter it, and a slow taker grows the heap without limit.
The Delayed contract should be consistent with equals/hashCode only if elements are removed by value; otherwise removal must go through the queue's own poll/remove semantics.
